unit_label: ABFM Module A unit 4 (courseware unit 4): staffing

facts.statement: Staffing: the process of recruiting and developing personnel to fill the roles in an organisation, covering personnel planning, procurement (selection and placement), training and development, performance evaluation and compensation; Peter Drucker is cited: of all the resources accessible to man, man can grow and develop. Functions: obtaining qualified individuals for positions; selecting the most qualified candidates (higher productivity and performance); promoting effective use of human resources; raising job satisfaction and morale; ensuring continued existence and expansion; placing people in the right jobs. Objectives: appropriate employees for appropriate positions; educating and cultivating human resources; designing policies on transfer and promotion; motivating towards better performance; positive employer-employee relations; meeting workers' demands so they are loyal; and positive interactions to keep morale strong.

Nature and salient features of staffing (courseware): concentrated on individuals; oriented towards development; all-pervasive; an ongoing procedure; human objectives; focus on both individuals and groups; creating an environment conducive to productive work; multidisciplinary character (sociology, anthropology, management, psychology; "human engineering"); an essential component of general management; a blend of art and science. Salient features: involvement with human beings; a distinct managerial function; a necessary activity at all managerial levels (managers remain ultimately responsible for hiring decisions even where a personnel department exists); associated with social responsibility; and affected by the internal and external environment (promotion, demotion and transfer policies internally; government policy and the educational environment externally).

Facets and significance of staffing: three primary facets: recruitment (a positive process that seeks to attract more people with suitable profiles to apply), selection (a procedure that eliminates candidates by reviewing applications and choosing the best fit; it rejects, unlike recruitment) and training (improves employees' knowledge, abilities and capacity for jobs). Significance: recognises competent staff (determining number of workers and assigning to positions); enhancement of overall performance; ongoing capability for survival and development (succession planning); optimal employment of available human resources (avoiding under-utilisation); and increased job satisfaction and positive morale.

Systems approach to staffing and the number of managers (courseware): staffing is an open system within the company, linked to the outside environment, and must consider internal factors (personnel policies, organisational climate, reward system). The management inventory compares needs with available talent; both external and internal sources are used for recruitment, selection, placement, promotion and termination; a performance review, career strategy and training and development are also components. Staffing affects leading and controlling (trained managers create an atmosphere where members achieve enterprise and personal goals; quality managers prevent large deviations). Factors affecting the number and types of managers: the size of the business, the complexity of the organisation structure, the plans for expansion and the rate of turnover of managerial personnel; no regulation governs the ratio of managers to total staff; structure can be modified so the number of managers rises or falls through expanding or contracting delegation of authority; qualifications of each individual must also be determined.

Recruitment (courseware): recruitment is finding potential applicants and encouraging them to apply for a vacancy; staffing is the process of hiring the most qualified. Stages: determining the need for hiring; conceiving a recruitment strategy; drafting a job description; publicising the position; recruiting candidates; examining applications; phone interview or initial screening; conducting interviews; evaluating candidates; background check; making a decision; checking references; making an offer; hiring; on-boarding. Types: internal recruiting (filling positions from current staff); retained recruiting (a recruiting firm is paid an upfront fee and the company commits to an exclusive partnership; one firm per vacancy); contingency recruiting (the firm is paid only when a candidate it represents is accepted); recruiting for staffing agencies (temporary or limited-time jobs); outplacement recruiting (help to former employees, usually employer-sponsored, to find new employment); and reverse recruiting (an employee is urged to seek employment with a business that is a better fit). Advice: search within the organisation before looking outside; contact passive applicants (not looking for a job); hire the person already excelling in similar jobs.

Selection process (courseware): selection is choosing from a shortlist. Steps: (1) preliminary interview (to exclude those unfit); (2) taking applications; (3) examining applications by a screening committee; (4) employment tests (IQ, aptitude, competence, personality tests); (5) formal interview ("the fifth and last significant step" in the courseware wording, though three more steps follow); (6) verification of references; (7) medical tests; (8) final selection and appointment (an appointment letter; terms of employment such as hours, remuneration and leave; commonly on probation). Importance: the careful selection and placement of staff determines success; rapid achievement of goals; fewer industrial accidents when the right technical staff are engaged; job satisfaction and output rise when people find work they excel at; and contented people tend to have good morale and motivation.

Training (courseware): training follows orientation and increases skills, capacities and knowledge so workers are better suited to certain jobs. Importance: new candidates learn the mission, vision, laws, regulations and working circumstances; current staff update skills; to keep up with changes in technology; and to prepare employees for promotion and higher responsibilities. Benefits: boosts employee morale (and reduces absenteeism and turnover); decreased requirement for supervision; reduction in the number of accidents; increased promotion chances; and increased productivity. Types: on-the-job training (learning by doing; job rotation, mentoring, temporary promotions; straightforward and cost efficient) and off-the-job training (in a setting that is not the normal place of work: workshops, seminars, conferences; expensive but effective for training many people quickly; also vestibule training, where the training place mimics actual working conditions).

Retention and development (courseware): effective retention practices: hiring (giving applicants an accurate preview of the work); socialisation (integration programmes); training and development; compensation and rewards (three options: be the industry leader in salary and awards; use a person-based compensation structure; make an obvious connection between retention and rewards, for example tying vacation hours to seniority, retention bonuses, stock options, or linking defined benefit payouts to years of service); fair supervision (the single most critical factor in whether an employee remains in the position, according to several studies); and employee involvement (engaged employees are happy in their jobs; the courseware cites a study in which highly engaged employees had a probability of quitting five times lower). Strategies: comprehensive strategies (organisation-wide tactics: changes to hiring, improving the working environment, raising base salary by market rates; data from research, effective practices and benchmarking surveys) and strategies directed at retention (using exit interviews, post-leave interviews, stay interviews, employee focus groups and predicted turnover studies to design targeted plans). Implementation: laying the groundwork (turnover analysis, benchmarking, needs assessment; creating a plan; carrying out the plan; examining the results), benchmarking, comparative analysis with other organisations (external benchmarking) and internal benchmarking (monitoring turnover rate over time). Common problems: absence of support from senior management and the impression that participating entails pointless busywork.

Knowledge management and the SECI model (courseware): knowledge management (KM) is the processes of generating, exchanging, utilising and managing information and knowledge. Benefits: accessible knowledge supports the development of products and services, shorter development cycles, creative endeavours, getting the most out of staff experience, access to concepts for jobs, problem solving, and management of physical assets and intellectual property. Technologies: software for group work, workflow management systems, content management systems, scheduling software and electronic communication; e-learning or a learning management system (LMS) is the foundation. The SECI model (Nonaka and Takeuchi) has four parts: socialisation (the initial component; constant flow of information and knowledge among employees; chat rooms and opportunities to communicate during study), externalisation (connecting the material from online courses to events in actual workplaces), combination (regularly updating and streamlining training with feedback and subject matter experts' input) and internalisation (the ultimate purpose: employees internalise the information so they can use skills immediately). Use of metrics to measure LMS success; managers' participation is among the most important aspects.

Performance appraisal (courseware): the periodic examination of an employee's contribution to a company in terms of both job performance and overall contribution, also known as annual review, performance review or evaluation; usually annual, semi-annual or quarterly. Types: top-down (manager evaluates), self-evaluation, peer assessment, 360-degree feedback (the participant, supervisor and peers) and negotiated appraisal (a mediator lets the subject present first, to reduce adversarial aspects). Objectives: comparing actual performance with the standard; maintaining records for compensation and salary structure; discovering strengths and limitations (for placement); assessing potential; giving feedback; guiding training requirements; and shaping employees' approach to their work. Advantages: easier promotion decisions; salary information; growth of staff; identification of training needs; improving selection; communicating performance to management; source of inspiration. Disadvantages: elements used to evaluate may be inaccurate or inappropriate; glossing over important aspects; attitude, capabilities and initiative are nebulous and hard to evaluate; and managers conducting appraisals may lack the qualifications. The appraisal is used for four purposes: to inform employees how they are rated; to decide eligibility for merit raises; to decide who needs additional training; and to decide who should be considered for promotion. Four primary methods: evaluation of subordinates by a superior, of superiors by subordinates, of a colleague by a group of peers, and of bosses by subordinates; graphic rating scales and behaviourally anchored rating scales are behaviour-oriented evaluation methods.

Methods of performance appraisal (courseware): past-oriented methods: rating scales (numerical scales for criteria such as dependability, initiative, output, attendance and attitude; advantages: adaptability, easy to use, low cost; disadvantage: the rater's biases); trait analysis (a checklist of yes/no statements; advantages: economy, ease of administration; disadvantage: raters' biases and improper weights); forced choice method (blocks of statements in which the rater must choose true or false; HR assesses; disadvantage: statements may be wrongly framed); forced distribution method (employees are clustered around a high point on a rating scale, assuming a normal distribution; disadvantage: the assumption is unrealistic and central tendency errors may occur); critical incidents method (supervisors record critical behaviours as they occur; advantages: feedback is easy, reduces recency bias; disadvantage: negative incidents may be prioritised and it may mean overly close supervision); confidential records (the Annual Confidential Report in government departments; secretive, feedback only for an adverse entry, highly subjective); and pen portrait (the assessor writes a description of the assessee; used by armies for cadets). Future-oriented methods: management by objectives (performance is rated against objectives; the MBO process: establish goals in a conference, set performance standards, assess performance through frequent reviews, identify reasons for shortfall and give feedback, establish new goals); assessment centre approach (several evaluators judge employee performance in several situations, mostly for first-level supervisory positions and promotion potential; uses in-basket exercises, role-playing, critical incident and leaderless group discussion; evaluators are experienced managers; each candidate is classified as more than acceptable, less than acceptable or unacceptable; a summary report and feedback); and behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS: five steps: generate critical incidents; develop performance dimensions (say 5 or 10 clusters); reallocate incidents (retained if generally 50 to 70 per cent of the group assigns it to the same cluster); scale the incidents; develop the final instrument with 6 or 7 incidents per dimension as behaviour anchors; advantages: more accurate judgement, clear standards, good feedback, independence of dimensions).

Key result areas and career strategy (courseware): Key Result or Responsibility Areas (KRAs) are general areas of outcomes or outputs for which the sector or department is responsible, derived from short-term objectives; the individual Performance and Development Plan has two components, the Performance Plan and the Individual Development Plan, built through a four-step process: agreeing on key results areas; agreeing on performance objectives; agreeing on key performance indicators and their associated performance targets; and agreeing on action plans. Performance appraisal for career strategy: informal appraisals (daily) and formal appraisals (once or twice yearly); a professional life plan involves the construction of a personal profile, the formulation of long-range personal and professional goals, analysis of risks and opportunities, analysis of personal strengths and weaknesses, strategic career alternatives, consistency testing and strategic choice, development of short-range career objectives and action plans, contingency plans, implementation and monitoring. Seven steps in career strategy (a career development plan is a list of long and short-term goals): in-depth analysis of values, strengths and motivators; awareness of advantages; research possibilities; developing expertise; developing a network; considering and evaluating alternatives; and taking action.

Human resource development (HRD) (courseware): HRD enhances the efficiency of individuals, groups and organisations through training, organisation and career advancement initiatives. Benefits: people become more capable; employees are more engaged when HRD is adequate; a culture of trust and respect; an accepting attitude toward change; improvement of teamwork; an efficiency culture; participation and sense of pride; data on employee programmes and policies that supports planning. Types: on-the-job training (learning tasks while performing the work), work shadowing (an employee watches another perform the duties), classroom or online education, and intellectual or professional growth (university or certification programmes, seminars). Managing generations: the top five practices: do not make assumptions; avoid labels; ensure regular review of your own biases; focus on the people around you rather than the trends; and acknowledge and celebrate the differences. Managing diversity: up to four generations at work (Baby Boomers to Generation Z); advantages of generation diversity: problem-solving, understanding diverse audiences, occasions for educational growth and mentorship.

Industrial relations, change, stress (courseware): industrial relations are the relations and interactions within an industry between labour and management, including relations between employees and superiors and among employees, union-management relations (collective ties between unions and management) and collective relations among employers' associations, labour unions and the government; healthy industrial relations need mutual respect, understanding, goodwill and acknowledgement of dignity; business cycles affect them (harmony in growth, poorer in recession). Management of change: managing the conversation between those leading the change and those implementing it, the organisational context and emotional connections; Lewin's three stages (unfreeze, change, refreeze) and Kotter's 8-step model are cited; the change process has preparation, implementation and follow-through; the manager understands the drivers of change (pressures from within, such as new leadership, or from outside, such as new technology or a new competitor), formulates a strategy, communicates clearly to those affected and is ready to overcome obstacles. Stress management refers to treatments and psychotherapies aimed at regulating a person's stress, particularly chronic stress; levels of stress can be measured using physiological tests; effective stress management is a key to a happy and successful life.

payload.title: What staffing is: functions and objectives

**Staffing** is **recruiting and developing the people** needed to fill an organisation's roles. It covers **personnel planning, procurement (selection and placement), training and development, performance evaluation and compensation**.

**Functions:** obtain **qualified people** for positions; select the **most qualified candidates** (higher productivity); use human resources **effectively**; raise **job satisfaction and morale**; secure the organisation's **continued existence and expansion**; put people in the **right jobs**.

**Objectives:** **right people for the right positions**; **educate and cultivate** human resources; design **policies on transfer and promotion**; **motivate** towards better performance; build **positive employer-employee relations**; meet workers' demands so they are **loyal**; keep **morale** strong.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites Drucker: of all the resources accessible to man, only man can grow and develop.

self_check.expected_takeaway: For example the right employees for the right positions, and developing human resources.

payload.title: Nature and salient features of staffing
payload.core_explanation_md:
